prompt: Explain how U.S. health insurance works using only fantasy football metaphors. Keep going long after the metaphor collapses.
response:
# U.S. Health Insurance: A Fantasy Football Explainer

## The Draft (Open Enrollment)

Once a year, there's a draft window. Miss it, and you're locked out until next season unless you have a "qualifying event" — like getting traded (new job), getting married (roster merger), or getting cut (losing coverage). You can't just wake up in Week 9 and decide you want a team. That's not how leagues work.

## Your Entry Fee (Premiums)

You pay a league fee every month just to have a roster. You pay this whether you set your lineup or not. You pay it if you're on a bye week. You pay it if you're in a coma. Especially if you're in a coma.

## The Deductible (The Points You Must Score Alone)

Here's the twist: even after paying your entry fee, the league doesn't start paying out until *you* personally score, say, 3,000 fantasy points out of pocket. Before that? Every waiver claim is full price. You're basically playing in a league that watches you play and takes notes.

## In-Network vs. Out-of-Network (Your League's Approved Player Pool)

You can only draft players from your league's approved list. Want Patrick Mahomes but he's not in your player pool? You can still start him, but it'll cost you 400% more and the commissioner might retroactively decide he was never eligible. Also, sometimes the *quarterback* is in-network but the *offensive line* isn't, and you find out via invoice.

## Prior Authorization (Asking the Commissioner If You're Allowed to Start Your Own Player)

Before starting your RB1 in a crucial matchup, you must fax — yes, fax — a request to the commissioner explaining why you need him. The commissioner, who has never watched football, may deny this because "a kicker would be more cost-effective." You can appeal. The appeal takes six weeks. The game was Sunday.

## Copays (The Toll Booth on Your Own Roster)

Every time you check your lineup, that's $30. Specialist lineup check (like asking about your tight end)? $75. Emergency lineup check on a Sunday? $500 and they might not even tell you the score.

---

## Where the Metaphor Starts Wheezing

Now — and stay with me — imagine your league is chosen by your *employer*, who negotiated it without asking you, and if you quit your job you lose your entire roster within 30 days unless you pay COBRA, which is like paying quadruple league fees to keep a team you already had.

Imagine your co-manager (spouse) can be on your roster, but the league charges per bench spot, and your children are automatically flex players until age 26, at which point they're released to free agency to find their own leagues, which they cannot afford, so they simply stop playing football and hope they never get tackled.

## Where the Metaphor Is Fully Dead and We're Dragging Its Body

Imagine your kicker is actually your pancreas. Your pancreas needs a procedure. The procedure is in-network. The anesthesiologist watching your pancreas is out-of-network, which you learn four months later via a bill for $12,000. You call the league office. You are on hold for two hours listening to smooth jazz. The representative tells you the claim was coded as "elective punt return" instead of "medically necessary field goal." You must dispute this. The dispute form asks for your league ID, your group number, your member number, and your pancreas's number, all of which are different numbers.

Imagine that scoring points *against yourself* is the only way to unlock league payouts, so the sicker your roster gets, the closer you are to "value," which is a sentence that should alarm everyone.

Imagine there's a special league for retired managers (Medicare) that has Parts A, B, C, and D, which are not sequential, do not do what you'd guess, and Part C is secretly just the regular leagues wearing a trench coat.

Imagine 27 million people simply don't have a team and are told to try the Emergency League, which cannot turn you away but will bill you the GDP of a small nation, per quarter, no huddle.

## Final Score

Fantasy football is a game where the rules are arcane, the scoring is arbitrary, everyone's angry at the commissioner, and you keep paying anyway because the alternative is unthinkable.

So actually, the metaphor never collapsed. It was load-bearing the whole time.
